[[File:3-generalized-2-cube_skew.svg|thumb|The [[3-3 duoprism|{3}×{3} duoprism]] is a proprism as the product of two orthogonal triangles, having 9 squares between pairs of edges of 2 sets of 3 triangles, and 18 vertices, as seen in this skew orthogonal projection.]]
In [[geometry]] of 4 dimensions or higher, a '''proprism''' is a [[polytope]] resulting from the [[Cartesian product]] of two or more polytopes, each of two dimensions or higher. The term was coined by [[John Horton Conway]] for ''product prism''. The dimension of the space of a proprism equals the sum of the dimensions of all its product elements. Proprisms are often seen as ''k''-face elements of [[uniform polytope]]s.<ref>[[John Horton Conway|John H. Conway]], Heidi Burgiel, Chaim Goodman-Strauss, ''The Symmetries of Things'' 2008, {{isbn|978-1-56881-220-5}} (Chapter 26, p.&nbsp;391 "proprism")</ref>

== Properties==
The number of [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]] in a proprism is equal to the product of the number of vertices in all the polytopes in the product.

The minimum [[symmetry order]] of a proprism is the product of the symmetry orders of all the polytopes. A higher symmetry order is possible if polytopes in the product are identical.

A proprism is [[Convex polytope|convex]] if all its product polytopes are convex.

== f-vectors==
An [[f-vector]] is a number of ''k''-face elements in a polytope from ''k''=0 (points) to ''k''=''n''−1 (facets). An extended f-vector can also include ''k''=−1 (nullitope), or ''k''=''n'' (body). Prism products include the body element. (The dual to prism products includes the nullitope, while pyramid products include both.)

The f-vector of prism product, A×B, can be computed as (f<sub>A</sub>,'''1''')*(f<sub>B</sub>,'''1'''), like [[polynomial multiplication]] polynomial coefficients.

For example for product of a triangle, f=(3,3), and dion, f=(2) makes a [[triangular prism]] with 6 vertices, 9 edges, and 5 faces:
:f<sub>A</sub>(x) = (3,3,'''1''') = 3 + 3x + x<sup>2</sup> (triangle)
:f<sub>B</sub>(x) = (2,'''1''') = 2 + x (dion)
:f<sub>A∨B</sub>(x) = f<sub>A</sub>(x) * f<sub>B</sub>(x)
::= (3 + 3x + x<sup>2</sup>) * (2 + x)
:: = 6 + 9x + 5x<sup>2</sup> + x<sup>3</sup>
:: = (6,9,5,'''1''')

[[Hypercube]] f-vectors can be computed as Cartesian products of ''n'' dions, {&nbsp;}<sup>n</sup>. Each {&nbsp;} has f=(2), extended to f=(2,'''1''').

For example, an [[8-cube]] will have extended f-vector power product: f=(2,'''1''')<sup>8</sup> = (4,4,'''1''')<sup>4</sup> = (16,32,24,8,'''1''')<sup>2</sup> = (256,1024,1792,1792,1120,448,112,16,'''1'''). If equal lengths, this doubling represents {&nbsp;}<sup>8</sup>, a square tetra-prism {4}<sup>4</sup>, a tesseract duo-prism {4,3,3}<sup>2</sup>, and regular 8-cube {4,3,3,3,3,3,3}.

== Double products or duoprisms==
{{See|Duoprism}}

In geometry of 4 dimensions or higher, '''duoprism''' is a [[polytope]] resulting from the [[Cartesian product]] of two polytopes, each of two dimensions or higher. The Cartesian product of an ''a''-polytope, a ''b''-polytope is an ''(a+b)''-polytope, where ''a'' and ''b'' are 2-polytopes ([[polygon]]) or higher.

Most commonly this refers to the product of two polygons in 4-dimensions. In the context of a product of polygons, Henry P. Manning's 1910 work explaining the [[Four-dimensional space|fourth dimension]] called these '''double prisms'''.<ref>''The Fourth Dimension Simply Explained'', Henry P. Manning, Munn & Company, 1910, New York. Available from the University of Virginia library. Also accessible online: [https://web.archive.org/web/20030121092141/http://etext.lib.virginia.edu/etcbin/toccer-new2?id=ManFour.sgm&images=images%2Fmodeng&data=%2Ftexts%2Fenglish%2Fmodeng%2Fparsed&tag=public&part=all The Fourth Dimension Simply Explained]&mdash;contains a description of duoprisms (double prisms) and duocylinders (double cylinders). [https://books.google.com/books?id=Y7cEAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Fourth+Dimension+Simply+Explained Googlebook]</ref>

The [[Cartesian product]] of two [[polygon]]s is the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of points:
:<math>P_1 \times P_2 = \{ (x,y,u,v) | (x,y)\in P_1, (u,v)\in P_2 \}</math>
where ''P<sub>1</sub>'' and ''P<sub>2</sub>'' are the sets of the points contained in the respective polygons.

The smallest is a [[3-3 duoprism]], made as the product of 2 triangles. If the triangles are regular it can be written as a product of [[Schläfli symbol]]s, {3}&nbsp;×&nbsp;{3}, and is composed of 9 vertices.

The [[tesseract]], can be constructed as the duoprism {4}&nbsp;×&nbsp;{4}, the product of two equal-size orthogonal [[square]]s, composed of 16 vertices. The [[5-cube]] can be constructed as a duoprism {4}&nbsp;×&nbsp;{4,3}, the product of a square and cube, while the [[6-cube]] can be constructed as the product of two cubes, {4,3}&nbsp;×&nbsp;{4,3}.

== Triple products ==
[[File:333-prism.png|thumb|The prism {3}&nbsp;×&nbsp;{3}&nbsp;×&nbsp;{3} can be seen in orthogonal projection within a regular enneagon.]]
In geometry of 6 dimensions or higher, a triple product is a [[polytope]] resulting from the [[Cartesian product]] of three polytopes, each of two dimensions or higher. The Cartesian product of an ''a''-polytope, a ''b''-polytope, and a ''c''-polytope is an (''a''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''b''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''c'')-polytope, where ''a'', ''b'' and ''c'' are 2-polytopes ([[polygon]]) or higher.

The lowest-dimensional forms are [[6-polytope]]s being the [[Cartesian product]] of three [[polygon]]s. The smallest can be written as {3}&nbsp;×&nbsp;{3}&nbsp;×&nbsp;{3} in [[Schläfli symbol]]s if they are regular, and contains 27 vertices. This is the product of three [[equilateral triangle]]s and is a [[uniform polytope]]. The f-vectors can be computed by (3,3,'''1''')<sup>3</sup> = (27,81,108,81,36,9,'''1''').

The [[6-cube]], can be constructed as a triple product {4}&nbsp;×&nbsp;{4}&nbsp;×&nbsp;{4}. The f-vectors can be computed by (4,4,'''1''')<sup>3</sup> = (64,192,240,160,60,12,'''1''').
